atoms.text: You will hear five people talking about politically correct language. First, read the statements. Then listen to the audio file and match each speaker (1 to 5) with one of the statements.
atoms.sound: You will hear five people talking about politically correct language. First reed the statements. Then listen to the audio file and match each speaker with one of the statements.

instruction.sound: speaker 1 <voice voiceLang='en' voice='f5Us_chirp'>Honestly, I’m mostly for it, but not in a preachy way. Like, if changing a couple words means someone doesn’t feel singled out, why wouldn’t I do that? I work in a clinic, and you see how language lands on people who already feel vulnerable. At the same time, I hate when it turns into a purity test online. I’m not trying to “perform” correctness—I’m just trying to be considerate.</voice> speaker 2 <voice voiceLang='en' voice='m1Us_chirp'>I’m kind of over it, if I’m blunt. It feels like everything’s “woke” now, and you’re one bad phrase away from getting dogpiled. So … you see … I’m not against being respectful—obviously. But a lot of this stuff comes off like status signaling, like, “look how enlightened I am.” Also, people use it to shut down debates rather than actually listen. If the intent isn’t hateful, I think we should relax a bit.</voice> speaker 3 <voice voiceLang='en' voice='f10Us_chirp'>I try, I really do, but sometimes I feel like the rules change faster than real life. My grandson corrects me, and I’m like—okay, teach me, fine. But it can get tense, like I’m being judged as a person, not just someone learning new terms. I grew up with expressions that were “normal” then and now they’re not. I don’t want to hurt anybody, yet I also don’t want to be scared to speak.</voice> speaker 4 <voice voiceLang='en' voice='m2In_chirp'>For me it’s practical. I moved here as an adult, so my English isn’t always smooth, and when people jump on wording, it feels unfair—like they’re grading my politics instead of my meaning. But I’ve also seen how certain labels can make people disappear in a conversation. So I aim for respectful language, especially at work, because it sets a tone. I just wish there was more patience and less “gotcha.”</voice> speaker 5 <voice voiceLang='en' voice='f12Us_chirp'>I’m torn. In my friend group, we’re pretty careful, and it honestly makes things feel safer. But at my job in marketing, the “inclusive language” training sometimes turns into corporate box-ticking. Like we swap words, but nothing changes for pay or hiring. So I don’t think PC language is pointless—it can be a signal of care—but I don’t love when it replaces real action. It’s… complicated.</voice>

So I don’t think PC language is pointless—it can be a signal of care—but I don’t love when it replaces real action. It’s… complicated.

sound/en/f5Us_chirp/Honestly, I’m mostly for it, but not in a preachy way. Like, if changing a couple words means someone doesn’t feel singled out, why wouldn’t I do that? I work in a clinic, and you see how language lands on people who already feel vulnerable. At the same time, I hate when it turns into a purity test online. I’m not trying to “perform” correctness—I’m just trying to be considerate.

sound/en/m1Us_chirp/I’m kind of over it, if I’m blunt. It feels like everything’s “woke” now, and you’re one bad phrase away from getting dogpiled. So … you see … I’m not against being respectful—obviously. But a lot of this stuff comes off like status signaling, like, “look how enlightened I am.” Also, people use it to shut down debates rather than actually listen. If the intent isn’t hateful, I think we should relax a bit.

sound/en/m2In_chirp/For me it’s practical. I moved here as an adult, so my English isn’t always smooth, and when people jump on wording, it feels unfair—like they’re grading my politics instead of my meaning. But I’ve also seen how certain labels can make people disappear in a conversation. So I aim for respectful language, especially at work, because it sets a tone. I just wish there was more patience and less “gotcha.”
